classification_signals: The paper proposes 'a theory to help understand and explain these effects' (abstract).
It introduces 'three different conceptions of being human' (Section 5) as a core conceptual framework.
It synthesizes a vast body of existing research (e.g., Ulrich, Kellert, Wilson, Alexander, Joye, Tsunetsugu) to support its theoretical propositions, rather than presenting new empirical data.
Appendix I provides 'Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design', which are practical applications derived from the theoretical framework.
The language is primarily argumentative and explanatory, building a coherent theoretical model for biophilic design and its neurological basis.
title: Neuroscience, the Natural Environment, and Building Design.

findings.antecedent: designs which connect humans to the lived experience
findings.consequent: overall sense of wellbeing, positive and therapeutic consequences on physiology
findings.quote: Empirical evidence confirms that designs which connect humans to the lived experience enhance our overall sense of wellbeing, with positive and therapeutic consequences on physiology.

findings.antecedent: imposing an artificial meaning on the built environment (by contemporary architects)
findings.consequent: contradiction of physical and natural processes, creation of inhuman buildings and cities (in form, scale, construction)
findings.quote: By imposing an artificial meaning on the built environment, contemporary architects contradict physical and natural processes, and thus create buildings and cities that are inhuman in their form, scale, and construction.

findings.antecedent: human neurological mechanism
findings.consequent: reaction to information field (transmission component) and physiological reaction in the body
findings.quote: Our neurological mechanism reacts to the information field (the transmission component), while inducing a reaction in the state of our body (the physiological component).

findings.antecedent: natural and built environments with intrinsic qualities
findings.consequent: strong sensory connection, healing
findings.quote: Both natural and built environments possess intrinsic qualities that enable such a strong connection, and which in turn can be healing.

findings.antecedent: certain types of information (innate hunger for)
findings.consequent: brain's pleasure centers activation, reduction of pain
findings.quote: Humans have an innate hunger for certain types of information: the circuits for this have been associated with the brain's pleasure centers, which also control the reduction of pain (Biederman & Vessel, 2006).

findings.antecedent: fractal qualities in our environment (ordered details arranged in a nested scaling hierarchy)
findings.consequent: human wellbeing
findings.quote: A growing amount of research finds that fractal qualities in our environment (i.e., ordered details arranged in a nested scaling hierarchy) contribute positively to human wellbeing (Hagerhall, Purcell & Taylor, 2004; Taylor, 2006; Taylor et. al., 2005).

findings.antecedent: natural environments (including artificial environments mimicking geometrical qualities of natural environments)
findings.consequent: hospital healing
findings.quote: Another direction of research has uncovered undisputed clinical advantages (faster hospital healing) of natural environments, including artificial environments mimicking geometrical qualities of natural environments (Frumkin, 2001; Ulrich, 1984; 2000).

findings.antecedent: viewing natural (or videos of natural) environments (in hospital settings)
findings.consequent: pain relief
findings.quote: Pain relief in hospital settings is significantly improved by viewing natural (or videos of natural) environments (Tse et. al., 2002), thus confirming the link between specific types of informational input and pain reduction.

findings.antecedent: neurologically-nourishing environment
findings.consequent: physiological (emotional) reaction
findings.quote: Reaction to a neurologically-nourishing environment is physiological (i.e. emotional) rather than intellectual.

findings.antecedent: innate information-processing system
findings.consequent: evolution along with physiology, acute tuning to visual complexity of natural environment, positive response to highest levels of organized complexity
findings.quote: There is mounting evidence of an innate information-processing system that has evolved along with the rest of our physiology (Joye, 2006; 2007a; 2007b). This system is acutely tuned to the visual complexity of the natural environment, specifically to respond positively to the highest levels of organized complexity (Salingaros, 2006).

findings.antecedent: presence and organization of information
findings.consequent: positive or negative effect on perceptive system
findings.quote: Not only the presence of information, but especially how that information is organized, produces a positive or negative effect on our perceptive system (Klinger & Salingaros, 2000; Salingaros, 2006).

findings.antecedent: ordered geometry of biological forms
findings.consequent: healing effects on human beings
findings.quote: We assume an underlying genetic factor as the basis for why the ordered geometry of biological forms connects with and leads to healing effects on human beings.

findings.antecedent: structures embodying organized complexity
findings.consequent: physiological and psychological connection (stronger than plain or disorganized complexity)
findings.quote: Human beings connect physiologically and psychologically to structures embodying organized complexity more strongly than to environments that are either too plain, or which present disorganized complexity (Salingaros, 2006).

findings.antecedent: connection process (with built/natural environment)
findings.consequent: health and mental wellbeing
findings.quote: The connection process (outlined in the following sections) plays a key role in our lives, because it influences our health and mental wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: contact with nature and complex geometry of natural forms
findings.consequent: complete and healthy life
findings.quote: Wilson's Biophilia Hypothesis asserts that we need contact with nature, and with the complex geometry of natural forms, just as much as we require nutrients and air for our metabolism (Kellert, 2005; Kellert & Wilson, 1993).

findings.antecedent: flat lawn (as visual purity/emptiness)
findings.consequent: senses perceive it as a single scale, inability to connect fractally
findings.quote: A flat lawn, by contrast, while better than a rectangular concrete slab, represents the same visual purity (emptiness) as the plain slab. Our senses perceive it as a single scale and are unable to connect to it fractally.

findings.antecedent: ecological complexity (interacting plants providing visual complexity)
findings.consequent: neurological nourishment
findings.quote: Nature exhibits ecological complexity: interacting plants that in turn provide visual complexity, which is a source of neurological nourishment.

findings.antecedent: industrial building-plus-garden (biological component grafted onto hostile armature)
findings.consequent: underlying neurological disconnection
findings.quote: The natural aspect of an industrial building-plus-garden is simply a biological component grafted onto an armature that is fundamentally hostile to human sensibilities. It still triggers an underlying neurological disconnection on a basic level.

findings.antecedent: neurological nourishment
findings.consequent: engagement with information and its organization
findings.quote: Neurological nourishment depends upon an engagement with information and its organization.

findings.antecedent: traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, shape of interior space
findings.consequent: informational connectivity, direct neurophysiology trigger (via geometrical connective rules)
findings.quote: Traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, and the shape of interior space helped to achieve informational connectivity. Long misinterpreted as a copy of natural forms, ornamentation in its deepest expressions is far more than that: it is a distillation of geometrical connective rules that trigger our neurophysiology directly.

findings.antecedent: underlying geometrical complexity of living structure (in biological organisms, artifacts, buildings)
findings.consequent: human nourishment
findings.quote: We, on the other hand, believe that the underlying geometrical complexity of living structure is what nourishes humans. This geometry could be equally expressed in biological organisms as in artifacts and buildings: the difference is merely one of degree (Alexander, 2002-2005).

findings.antecedent: built environment that is neurologically non-nourishing
findings.consequent: negative reaction, physical anxiety and distress
findings.quote: Therefore, we will instinctively react in a negative manner to a built environment that is neurologically non-nourishing, or which might actually cause physical anxiety and distress.

findings.antecedent: geometry of the environment (in hospital design)
findings.consequent: patient healing time
findings.quote: In hospital design, the geometry of the environment plays a significant role in how long it takes for a patient to be cured. Roger Ulrich has done pioneering work in this topic (Ulrich, 1984; 2000).

findings.antecedent: fine detail, contrast, symmetries, color, and connections (visual elements found in nature and traditional architectures)
findings.consequent: human perception engagement, positive physiology, mental health, sense of wellbeing
findings.quote: Our eye/brain system has evolved to perceive fine detail, contrast, symmetries, color, and connections. Symmetry, visual connections, ornament, and fine detail are necessary on buildings; not for any stylistic reason, but because our perception is built to engage with those features (Enquist & Arak, 1994; Salingaros, 2003; 2006). Creating an environment that deliberately eschews these elements... has negative consequences for our physiology, and thus for our mental health and sense of wellbeing (Joye, 2006; 2007a; 2007b; Kellert, 2005).

findings.antecedent: colorless, drab, minimalist surfaces and spaces
findings.consequent: mimicry of clinical symptoms of macular degeneration, stroke, cerebral achromatopsia, visual agnosia
findings.quote: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information mimic signs of human pathology. For example, colorless, drab, minimalist surfaces and spaces reproduce clinical symptoms of macular degeneration, stroke, cerebral achromatopsia, and visual agnosia (Salingaros, 2003; 2006).

findings.antecedent: drab, monotonous, and minimalist environments
findings.consequent: anxious sensation, sensory deprivation, neurophysiologic breakdown
findings.quote: We feel anxious in such environments, because they provoke in us a similar sensation as sensory deprivation and neurophysiologic breakdown.

findings.antecedent: naturalistic and stimulating habitats (for zoo animals)
findings.consequent: animals' psychological and social well-being
findings.quote: Judith Heerwagen has studied zoo animal behavior in naturalistic versus more artificial environments (Heerwagen, 2005). Starting from substantial observations of zoo animals, she reports the results of implementing a transformation towards more naturalistic habitats. As a consequence, the animals' psychological and social well-being has been drastically improved.

findings.antecedent: complexity and stimulation in the environment (for developing animals)
findings.consequent: increased intelligence, brain size, neural connectivity (up to 20%)
findings.quote: Incontrovertible results are obtained with young rats raised in information-rich environments, whose brains increase in size, and can improve their neural connectivity by up to 20% (Squire & Kandel, 1999: page 200).

findings.antecedent: room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail
findings.consequent: physiological response (positive)
findings.quote: physiological monitors recorded a marked response in favor of the room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail (Tsunetsugu, Miyazaki & Sato, 2005).

findings.antecedent: room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail vs. plain room
findings.consequent: expressed preference
findings.quote: In a clinical comparison of two distinct environments, one a plain room, and the other with wooden beams added to create hierarchical scaling, the subjects did not express any preference.

findings.antecedent: patterns recognized by neurophysiologic apparatus
findings.consequent: understanding humanity and its connection to the universe
findings.quote: Patterns recognized by our neurophysiologic apparatus are a key to understanding humanity and its connection to the universe.

findings.antecedent: sensory input
findings.consequent: emotional learning (subconscious, nondeclarative memory)
findings.quote: Emotional learning is the result of sensory input, but remains subconscious (i.e. stored in nondeclarative memory).

findings.antecedent: patterns learned emotionally through perception
findings.consequent: positive emotion (due to satisfying an internal template)
findings.quote: Patterns learned emotionally through perception act in the same way as inherited (genetically-based) responses. The reason they evoke a positive emotion to begin with, is because they satisfy an internal template.

findings.antecedent: Alexander's Pattern Language
findings.consequent: codification of evolved patterns of human-environment interaction, practical combinatoric framework for design
findings.quote: Christopher Alexander's Pattern Language codified evolved patterns of how humans interact with their environment and with each other (Alexander et. al., 1977). This prescient book established a practical combinatoric framework for design, based on evolved solutions.

findings.antecedent: architectural and urban patterns combining social and geometrical elements
findings.consequent: spontaneous emergence in different cultures and times (evolutionary result of typological exploration)
findings.quote: In the same way, a small number of architectural and urban patterns combining social and geometrical elements have arisen spontaneously in different cultures and in different times. Their appearance is evolutionary, since they are the end result of typological exploration via trial-and-error over generations.

findings.antecedent: programs that mimic patterns of speech, movement, and behavior (in robots)
findings.consequent: emulation of human qualities and emotions, observer interaction through specific complexity
findings.quote: it is possible to emulate human qualities and emotions, at least partially, by means of programs that mimic patterns of speech, movement, and behavior. The observer interacts through patterns of a very specific type of complexity that is characteristic of living, and specifically human, beings.

findings.antecedent: increasing complexity of interaction (in definite direction detectable by neurophysiology)
findings.consequent: higher degrees of human connectivity
findings.quote: Increasing the complexity of interaction in a definite direction (defined precisely by what our neurophysiology and sensory apparatus are built to detect) eventually leads to higher degrees of human connectivity.

findings.antecedent: contact with domestic animals
findings.consequent: positive emotional and health effects
findings.quote: Since the beginnings of history, people have benefited from (and documented) the positive emotional and health effects of contact with domestic animals.

findings.antecedent: abstract forms of architecture (lacking informational coding)
findings.consequent: insufficient information for neurological hardware processes, human detachment from perceivable world
findings.quote: The processes at work in our neurological hardware require a far greater degree of information than the abstract forms of architecture currently provide. Informational coding is missing from today's architecture. Within the intentional condition of contemporary architectural environments we are detached from the perceivable world.

findings.antecedent: deep connection with each other, living beings, and nature
findings.consequent: experience of wonder at the Creation
findings.quote: People experienced a deep connection with each other, with living beings, and with nature. They experienced a wonder at the Creation (Wilson, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Alexander's work on fundamental geometrical properties
findings.consequent: understanding of underlying and far-reaching interconnectedness, realization of loss of fundamental connectivity in 20th century architecture/urbanism
findings.quote: Christopher Alexander (2002-2005) raises the same issue about our loss of fundamental connectivity, in the context of architecture and urbanism. Alexander argues for an underlying and far-reaching interconnectedness based upon fundamental geometrical properties.

findings.antecedent: physical matter with very special informational configurations
findings.consequent: transcendence of inert materiality, endowment with characteristics of life
findings.quote: Physical matter does transcend its inert materiality through very special informational configurations. This process can endow physical forms with the characteristics of life

findings.antecedent: religious architecture of the past
findings.consequent: achievement of connective experience, material transcendence
findings.quote: Religious architecture of the past helps us to achieve this type of connective experience; indeed, that was its original purpose.

findings.antecedent: conscious work with mechanism of informational exchange
findings.consequent: re-creation of intensely connective buildings, highest level of neurological nourishment
findings.quote: Consciously working with the mechanism of informational exchange, we can re-create buildings having the same intense degree of connection. Such buildings will provide the highest level of neurological nourishment.

findings.antecedent: natural geometry in living structure
findings.consequent: manifestation of God
findings.quote: God is manifest in a natural geometry in living structure (Alexander, 2002-2005).

findings.antecedent: human beings
findings.consequent: evolved ability and need to process information embedded in their environment
findings.quote: Human beings have evolved the ability and the need to process information embedded in their environment.

findings.antecedent: biophilic design
findings.consequent: re-orientation of architecture towards a world governed by coherent information, thinking on many levels of complexity
findings.quote: Biophilic design re-orients architecture towards a world governed by coherent information; it also leads people to think on many levels of complexity (which is the way nature works).

findings.antecedent: natural and traditional built environments rich in informational content
findings.consequent: more intrinsically human place
findings.quote: The natural and traditional built environments rich in informational content make a place more intrinsically human.

findings.antecedent: emphasis on informational content (in built environment)
findings.consequent: neurological connection at human scale, emotional nourishment
findings.quote: By emphasizing informational content, we can shape the built environment according to the constituent logic and order necessary to provide neurological connection at a human scale and thus emotional nourishment.

findings.antecedent: smallest perceivable scale (microstructure of natural materials, fine-grained texture/ornament)
findings.consequent: ordered complexity, accessibility to human contact
findings.quote: The smallest perceivable scale is established with either the microstructure of natural materials, or by using very fine-grained texture/ornament. The ordered complexity of natural structure cannot easily be duplicated on this scale. The region containing fine detail has to be immediately accessible to human contact (and not lost at a distance).

findings.antecedent: definite scaling hierarchy (elements on next larger scale roughly 2-5 times larger than smaller scale)
findings.consequent: adaptation to human sensibilities
findings.quote: Design that adapts to human sensibilities should have a very definite scaling hierarchy. Obvious differentiated subdivisions or components need to obey a scaling rule, where elements on the next larger scale are roughly 3 times (more accurately, 2.7 times) larger than those on the immediately smaller scale.

findings.antecedent: richness of subsymmetries on smaller and intermediate scales
findings.consequent: visual coherence, connective symmetry
findings.quote: Symmetry is essential in design, not as expressed by an overall scale, but rather by the richness of subsymmetries on smaller and intermediate scales. Connective symmetry is an extensive quality, ideally acting throughout all levels of a scaling hierarchy. The density of subsymmetries, and their intensity of interaction inside a particular scale and across distinct scales, is what leads to visual coherence.

findings.antecedent: construction systems that preserve natural materials for visible surfaces (e.g., wood grain, soft acoustical properties)
findings.consequent: informational load, human connection (through sense or touch)
findings.quote: Innovative architects can and should develop new structural systems, which preserve natural materials for the visible surfaces, to be used in regions that human beings can directly access through sense or touch.

findings.antecedent: industrial modular production of ornamental panels and building components (e.g., Islamic tiling, Guimard, Sullivan, Wright)
findings.consequent: effective extension of neurologically-engaging patterns, high degree of encoded information, human wellbeing
findings.quote: Going back to the precedent of Islamic tiling patterns, industrial modules such as those used by Hector Guimard, Louis Sullivan, and Frank Lloyd Wright represent an effective extension of the requisite types of neurologically-engaging patterns. Though it hasn't been used for many decades, this form of architectural expression contains a high degree of encoded information and is thus very useful for establishing human wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: re-use of natural materials from older buildings, incorporating architectural salvage
findings.consequent: establishment of scaling hierarchy, high informational content
findings.quote: Architects must train their eye to look for those materials that help to establish the scaling hierarchy and deliver a high informational content. Every consideration should be given to incorporating materials found in architectural salvage yards into new buildings.

findings.antecedent: concrete molded with ordered patterns (vs. random texture or flat panel)
findings.consequent: positive sensory feedback, natural surface (visual and tactile)
findings.quote: Instead of letting its surface present either a random texture or an unfriendly flat panel, we can mold it with patterns (as did Frank Lloyd Wright). Unfinished concrete has an informationally frustrating surface because it lacks ordered microstructure. We could moderate the unfriendly surface of raw concrete with a permanent surface or aggregate added while the concrete is still wet (a pioneer in this technique is Antoni Gaudí). On the other hand, using wooden planks to form the concrete does leave a wood grain impression, but this does not produce a visually-coherent surface because it does not have the correct fractal scaling into microstructure, and at best seems unnatural. We have in mind more ordered patterns formed into the concrete, as well as a more “natural” surface, both visual and tactile.

findings.antecedent: free hand to workmen (e.g., laying out tiles, adjusting window dimensions), craft of building recognized
findings.consequent: most pleasurable feedback, extension of natural structure's infinite and subtle variation into construction materials/methods, architecture imbued with life
findings.quote: Whenever possible, we should give free hand to the workmen to find their own expression, such as in laying out tiles and adjusting dimensions of a window. The craft of building should once again be recognized, and craftsmen should be given the authority to mold the smaller scales of the building as it develops, so as to foster the most pleasurable feedback as they see it. Natural structure shows an infinite and subtle variation, and this potential should be extended into the use of construction materials and methods. Expression through materials requires an intimate working knowledge of the nature of these materials. This freedom extends the design process out of the hands of the architect, and was practiced in recent times by Friedrich Hundertwasser. By allowing individual input in this manner, we imbue the architecture with a life outside the frozen expression typically conceived on the drawing board.

findings.antecedent: robotic manufacturing programmed to emulate variations in physical mechanics of material placement
findings.consequent: components and materials endowed with similar degree of life as pre-industrial buildings, enormous variation
findings.quote: We can program robotic fabricators to emulate the variations in the physical mechanics of material placement, so as to endow components and materials with a similar degree of life found in pre-industrial buildings. The technology exists to create an enormous variation, which can serve in the same way as individual hands-on design created by human craftsmen.

findings.antecedent: geometrical interweaving of plant life and natural features with building fabric, meandering/crenellated boundary, indoor garden, complex piece of nature (1-2 meters in size)
findings.consequent: biophilic design on room scale, substantial difference to biophilic connection
findings.quote: One is geometrical interweaving of plant life and natural features with the fabric of the building itself. We abandon the rectangular or convex footprint of a building, for a more meandering or crenellated boundary that partially surrounds gardens, verandas, and patios. If the building is large enough, then an indoor garden is possible. We focus here on a key concept. Intensify a fairly intimate scale: a complex piece of nature existing on the scale of a human being (1-2 meters in size) can make a substantial difference to our biophilic connection.

findings.antecedent: natural connective geometry (native plants growing wild)
findings.consequent: human health and wellbeing
findings.quote: Native plants growing wild define a particular complex geometry, and this is the geometry that can best serve to keep us healthy and make us well.

findings.antecedent: development of natural geometry and life on buildings (via weathering, invasion of plants)
findings.consequent: increasing life (vs. decay)
findings.quote: The development of a natural geometry and life on buildings, via weathering, and via the invasion of plants, is nowadays seen as an unwelcome intrusion as a sign of decay. We, on the contrary, see these as symptoms of increasing life.

findings.antecedent: urban geometry permitting pedestrian access to plant life, coherently designed gardens
findings.consequent: human interaction with nature, enjoyment
findings.quote: Human beings can interact with nature only if the urban geometry permits such interactions. In addition to visual line-of-sight, we pay attention to pedestrian access and the formation of urban space. Having some plant life available is only a first step: we need to make it accessible to pedestrians and design an environment in which such an interaction can be maintained and enjoyed.

findings.antecedent: suburban space (vast expanses of flat lawn and asphalt, exposed sidewalks, out-of-bounds private lawns, protective bushes/trees)
findings.consequent: psychologically-hostile environment for pedestrian
findings.quote: The worst disaster is suburban space, in which vast expanses of flat lawn and asphalt define a psychologically-hostile environment for the pedestrian. Sidewalks are exposed in the middle of this space, between the asphalt road and the forbidden lawn. Private lawns are out-of-bounds, while any bushes and trees form a protective wall around a house, instead of belonging to the public realm.

findings.antecedent: distribution of units/uses away from uniformity, many complex natural areas, natural (fractal) distribution of sizes for green spaces
findings.consequent: visual and biological complexity, internal complexity and variety
findings.quote: On the broader urban scale, we should again focus any distribution of units or uses away from a uniformity that privileges the largest scale. Moving away from large, purely decorative lawns, we try and design many complex natural areas; resisting the amalgamation of every plant into one "park"; resisting the alignment of everything according to a simplistic geometry; and avoiding the homogenization of green spaces to a single plant species. We should seek instead to preserve and reproduce visual and biological complexity such as is found in natural environments. A natural (fractal) distribution of sizes applied to green spaces in the city implies the existence of very many small ones, several ones of intermediate size, and only a few large ones. Each of these green spaces should in turn have its own internal distribution, which can be achieved only by having internal complexity and variety.

findings.antecedent: Alexander's Pattern Language framework
findings.consequent: anticipation and support of biophilic design, generation of environments adapted to human sensibilities
findings.quote: A common thread running through Alexander's work is the need to connect human beings with nature, looking to nature as a source of mental and physical nourishment. That work anticipates and supports biophilic design.

limitations: There are clearly unknown factors playing a role yet to be discovered in human response to design (p. 4).
Not all of the universe's mysteries are open to human comprehension (p. 20).
minimum_safe_summary: This paper proposes a conceptual framework for understanding the neurological basis of biophilic design, arguing that human beings have evolved to require specific informational input from their environment for health and wellbeing. It synthesizes existing research to show that natural and traditional built environments, characterized by organized complexity, fractal qualities, and hierarchical scaling, provide 'neurological nourishment' that positively impacts physiology, mental health, and emotional states. Conversely, minimalist or information-poor environments can lead to anxiety and physiological distress. The paper advocates for an architecture that consciously incorporates these natural geometries and fosters deep human-environment connections, moving beyond abstract design to create spaces that are intrinsically human and healing.
